stories.title: Build an AI software factory with seven specialized agents
stories.summary: Turn one product brief into reviewed, tested, releasable software by assigning seven agents clear roles and making every handoff an artifact. This practical setup uses isolated worktrees, dependency-aware tasks, explicit quality gates, and a human-controlled release step.
stories.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems fail when every agent edits everything or communicates only through chat. Role boundaries, durable artifacts, and automated gates make parallel work understandable, recoverable, and safe enough to reuse.
whatToWatch: Start with one small vertical slice before allowing parallel implementation
Give each agent one owned scope and require evidence with every handoff
Keep deployment, secrets, destructive operations, and final approval human-controlled
questions: Which repository workflow should you automate first?
What checks must pass before an agent can hand work to the next stage?
Which actions in your environment must always require human approval?

tutorial.outcome: A working seven-agent pipeline that takes a scoped issue through architecture, implementation, verification, review, and a human-approved release.
prerequisites: A Git repository with a repeatable build and test command
An agent-capable coding CLI with permission limited to the repository
A task tracker or structured state store for dependencies and status
CI checks that can block merging when tests, types, lint, or security checks fail

steps.title: Turn the request into an executable brief
steps.instruction: Collect the user outcome, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and measurable acceptance criteria. Refuse to proceed when a product decision changes behavior and has no answer.
steps.deliverable: brief.md or an issue containing scope, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and open decisions.
steps.prompt: Convert this request into a one-page implementation brief. Separate facts, assumptions, open decisions, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. Do not propose code yet.

steps.title: Map the system and contracts
steps.instruction: Inspect the repository, identify affected components and data contracts, find existing patterns to reuse, and document risks. Define interfaces before implementation details.
steps.deliverable: A change map listing files, APIs, schemas, dependencies, migrations, and rollback concerns.
steps.prompt: Read the brief and repository. Produce the smallest architecture that satisfies it, identify existing helpers to reuse, and list every contract that must remain backward compatible.

steps.title: Build a dependency-aware task graph
steps.instruction: Split the architecture into independently owned tasks. Mark dependencies, expected files, completion evidence, and integration order. Parallelize only tasks that do not edit the same surface.
steps.deliverable: A task graph with owners, dependencies, file scopes, and verification commands.
steps.prompt: Create executable tasks from the architecture. Each task must have one owner, a non-overlapping file scope, dependencies, a definition of done, and an exact verification command.

steps.title: Implement in an isolated worktree
steps.instruction: Create a branch or worktree for one ready task, make surgical changes, follow repository conventions, and commit only owned files. Return the diff, assumptions, and command results.
steps.deliverable: A focused commit with code, tests, and a short handoff containing evidence.
steps.prompt: Own only this task and file scope. Implement the complete behavior, add focused tests, run the listed checks, and return the commit SHA plus any assumptions or remaining risks.

steps.title: Prove behavior independently
steps.instruction: Test the acceptance criteria rather than trusting the implementation report. Exercise success, failure, malformed input, concurrency, persistence, and upgrade paths that apply.
steps.deliverable: A verification report with commands, observed results, and reproducible failures.
steps.prompt: Treat the implementation as untrusted. Verify every acceptance criterion and the highest-risk edge cases. Report only reproducible failures with exact commands and evidence.

steps.title: Review correctness and security
steps.instruction: Review the actual diff and surrounding call paths for logic errors, security boundaries, data loss, compatibility, and missing cleanup. Ignore style unless it creates risk.
steps.deliverable: A short list of high-confidence findings, each tied to a file, line, impact, and fix.
steps.prompt: Review this diff against the brief and repository contracts. Find only high-confidence correctness, security, compatibility, or data-loss issues. Explain impact and the smallest safe fix.

steps.title: Integrate, release, and observe
steps.instruction: Rebase onto the target branch, rerun gates on the integrated result, produce release notes and a rollback plan, then pause for human approval before merge or deployment. After release, check health and error signals.
steps.deliverable: A merge-ready change, release checklist, rollback command, and post-release observation report.
steps.prompt: Prepare the integrated release candidate. Re-run all required gates, summarize user-visible changes and risks, provide rollback steps, and stop before merge or deployment until a human approves.

qualityGates: No task starts without acceptance criteria and an owned file scope
No handoff is accepted without a diff or artifact plus command evidence
No merge occurs when required tests, type checks, lint, or security checks fail
The verifier and reviewer must not be the implementation agent
Deployment and destructive actions require explicit human approval
costControls: Use a smaller model for discovery, planning, and routine verification; reserve stronger models for architecture and difficult reviews
Cap retries and stop agents that repeat the same failed approach
Pass focused files and artifacts instead of the entire conversation
Parallelize independent tasks only; duplicate agents reviewing the same scope waste tokens
Record per-task runtime and token cost so expensive stages can be redesigned

stories.title: Position Paper Argues LLMs Fundamentally Can't 'Jump'
stories.summary: A position paper titled "Position: LLMs Can't Jump" is circulating and being discussed on Hacker News. The piece appears to argue that large language models have a structural limitation preventing a certain kind of reasoning or capability leap, though the specifics beyond the title aren't detailed in what's been shared.
stories.whyItMatters: Position papers like this shape how researchers and practitioners frame the current ceiling on LLM capabilities, feeding into broader debates about scaling versus fundamental architectural limits.
whatToWatch: Whether the paper gains traction or rebuttals from other researchers
Any follow-up commentary clarifying the specific limitation being described
questions: What exactly does "jump" refer to in this context — a reasoning task, a benchmark, or a capability class?
Is this empirical or purely argumentative/theoretical?

stories.title: Oracle Cuts Its Always Free ARM Compute Allowance in Half
stories.summary: Oracle Cloud has reportedly reduced the resources available under its "Always Free" ARM-based compute tier, according to a blog post highlighted on Hacker News. The change affects developers who relied on the free tier for low-cost ARM instances.
stories.whyItMatters: Free ARM compute has been a popular option for hobbyists and small teams running lightweight inference and side projects, so a cut shrinks a low-cost entry point into cloud-based AI experimentation.
whatToWatch: Whether Oracle issues an official statement or FAQ on the new limits
Any migration scramble from users moving workloads to other free-tier providers
questions: Does this apply retroactively to existing free-tier accounts or only new sign-ups?
What's driving the reduction — cost, abuse, or capacity constraints?

sources.title: Oracle Just Halved Its Always Free ARM Limits

stories.title: Show HN Pitches a Fund Blending Tokenized Gold, Tech Stocks, and Digital Assets
stories.summary: A Hacker News "Show HN" post floats the idea of a single fund holding a mix of tokenized gold, tech stocks, and digital assets. Details beyond the concept pitch itself aren't available from the supplied source.
stories.whyItMatters: It's more a fintech/tokenization concept than an AI story, but it signals continued experimentation with blending traditional and crypto-native asset wrappers around tech-heavy portfolios.
whatToWatch: Whether the concept moves from a Show HN pitch to an actual launched product
Community reaction and regulatory questions raised in the discussion
questions: Who is behind this and is it a live product or just a proposal?
What regulatory framework, if any, would govern such a tokenized fund?

stories.title: The Rust Project Is Adopting a Formal LLM Policy
stories.summary: The rust-lang/rust project is putting in place a policy governing the use of LLMs in its development process, per a post highlighted on Hacker News. The move formalizes how AI-assisted contributions will be handled within one of the most widely used open-source language projects.
stories.whyItMatters: As major open-source projects set explicit rules for AI-generated code and contributions, their policies often become reference points for how other maintainers approach the same question.
whatToWatch: The specific rules the policy sets for disclosure, review, or use of LLM-generated code
Whether other large open-source projects adopt similar policies following Rust's lead
questions: Does the policy restrict LLM use in contributions, reviews, or both?
Is this a response to a specific incident or a proactive governance move?

stories.title: New Research Proposes 'Zero-Token' Memory Operations for LLM Agents
stories.summary: A paper posted to arXiv, titled "Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents," describes an approach for handling agent memory without consuming additional token budget. It was surfaced via Hacker News; no further technical detail is available beyond the title.
stories.whyItMatters: Memory handling is a persistent cost and design bottleneck for LLM agents, so techniques that reduce token overhead could meaningfully cut the cost of running long-lived or context-heavy agents.
whatToWatch: Whether the method is adopted or tested by agent frameworks in practice
Independent benchmarking against existing memory approaches
questions: How does "zero-token" memory actually work mechanically — is it offloaded to external storage or a separate model call?
What tradeoffs (latency, accuracy) does it introduce?

stories.title: An SLM trained on $8 ESP32-S3
stories.summary: A GitHub project demonstrates a small language model (SLM) trained on and for the ESP32-S3, a microcontroller that costs around $8, according to a post shared on Hacker News. It's an edge-AI proof-of-concept rather than a commercial product.
stories.whyItMatters: Projects like this illustrate how far model miniaturization has come, pointing toward a future where cheap, ubiquitous hardware can run useful AI locally without cloud dependence.
whatToWatch: Whether the project gains a following and gets extended to other low-cost microcontrollers
Any benchmarks on what tasks the model can realistically perform
questions: What can the resulting model actually do, and how does its quality compare to cloud-hosted small models?
Is this reproducible by others without specialized hardware knowledge?

stories.title: OpenAI Publishes Index of Third-Party Cyber Evaluations of Its Models
stories.summary: OpenAI released an index covering third-party cybersecurity evaluations conducted on its models. The publication appears to catalog independent assessments of cyber-related risks or capabilities tied to OpenAI's model lineup.
stories.whyItMatters: External evaluation of AI models' offensive cyber capability is a key plank of AI safety governance, and OpenAI publishing this signals continued emphasis on third-party scrutiny ahead of any regulatory requirements.
whatToWatch: Whether other frontier labs follow with similar public evaluation indexes
Any specific findings or risk flags that emerge from the cataloged evaluations
questions: Which third parties conducted the evaluations and what methodology did they use?
Do any of the evaluations flag capabilities that triggered mitigations or model changes?

stories.title: AI Infra Debate: Are 'Megakernels' Back in Fashion?
stories.summary: Latent Space's AI News roundup covers a resurgence of interest in "megakernels" — a GPU kernel-fusion approach to speeding up model execution — after the technique had reportedly fallen out of favor. The piece frames it as a back-and-forth trend within AI infrastructure engineering circles.
stories.whyItMatters: Low-level inference optimization techniques like kernel fusion directly affect the cost and speed of running large models at scale, making them a quiet but consequential thread in the competitive infrastructure race.
whatToWatch: Whether major inference providers publicly adopt megakernel approaches
Follow-up technical writeups quantifying performance gains
questions: What specifically caused megakernels to fall out of favor before this resurgence?
Which companies or open-source projects are driving the renewed interest?

stories.title: Flowise, the Low-Code AI Agent Builder, Is Shutting Down
stories.summary: Flowise, a platform for visually building LLM and AI agent workflows, is shutting down, according to a post highlighted on Hacker News. No additional detail on the reasons or timeline is available beyond the announcement itself.
stories.whyItMatters: The shutdown of a known no-code/low-code AI agent tool is a data point on the competitive pressure facing smaller players in the crowded agent-tooling space, likely squeezed by well-funded platforms and built-in offerings from major labs.
whatToWatch: Whether Flowise offers a migration path or open-sources its remaining codebase
What existing users and integrators plan to switch to
questions: What specifically drove the shutdown — funding, competition, or acquisition?
Will the project's open-source components continue to be maintained by the community?

stories.title: Inside ChatGPT Work: OpenAI's Push for an Agent at Billion-User Scale
stories.summary: A Latent Space piece unpacks "ChatGPT Work," describing it as an agent aimed at serving a billion users. The analysis digs into what the product represents for OpenAI's enterprise and mass-market ambitions, based on the framing given in the piece.
stories.whyItMatters: If OpenAI is positioning an agent product for billion-user scale, it underscores how central agentic features have become to the company's growth strategy beyond the core chatbot experience.
whatToWatch: Rollout pace and which user segments (enterprise vs. consumer) get access first
Competitive responses from Google, Anthropic, and Microsoft on similar agent products
questions: What distinguishes ChatGPT Work technically or functionally from prior ChatGPT enterprise offerings?
Is "a billion users" an actual near-term target or aspirational framing?

stories.title: New Open-Source Tool 'Homebench' Benchmarks Local LLMs
stories.summary: A GitHub project called Homebench offers a benchmark suite for evaluating locally run LLMs on speed, memory usage, and output quality, per a post shared on Hacker News. It's aimed at people running models on their own hardware rather than via cloud APIs.
stories.whyItMatters: As more capable open-weight models become runnable on consumer hardware, standardized local benchmarking tools help users make informed tradeoffs between model choice and hardware constraints.
whatToWatch: Community adoption and contributed benchmark results across different hardware setups
Whether it becomes a reference point cited alongside other local-LLM leaderboards
questions: Which models and hardware configurations does it currently support?
How does its quality scoring methodology work?
